title: Annotatio IV §.VII: Origen — impropriety and real presence; presence and participation merely spiritual
pass_a_gloss: More rightly the next Doctor of the same age — Origen, celebrated among Theologians as much for a truly sublime exposition of many sacred Truths as he is not less full of certain more outstanding errors because of allegorical Interpretations of the Scriptures justly too frequent — not only established, after Tertullian’s example, the impropriety of Christ’s words This is my body together with the real presence of Christ’s body in the Sacred Supper, but moreover urges that this presence of Christ’s body, nay also the participation, is merely Spiritual; on the former arguing thus against the Marcionites: But if Christ (as the Marcionites object) was destitute of flesh and bloodless, of what sort of Flesh, of what body, of what blood finally did He minister the signs and IMAGES BREAD AND CUP? Dialogue 3 on the Man Christ.
pass_b_english: Next, Origen (same century): with Tertullian he stabilizes the impropriety of ‘This is my body’ and real presence — then urges that presence and participation are merely Spiritual.
Against Marcionites: if Christ had no flesh and blood, of what flesh and blood did He minister bread and cup as signs and IMAGES?
source_text: Rectius Seculi ejusdem Doctor proximus, utut non minus, ob allegoricas Scripturarum Interpretationes justo crebriores, erroribus aliquot exstantioribus scatentes, quàm ob multarum Veritatum sacrarum expositionem verè sublimem, famâ inter Theologos celebratus, ORIGENES puta, non improprietatem tantùm verborum Christi: Hoc est corpus meum, unà cum præsentia corporis Christi reali, in S. Cœna, ad exemplum Tertulliani, stabilivit, sed verò prætereà hanc corporis Christi præsentiam, quin & participationem, merè Spiritualem urget esse; de priori, ita adversus Marcionitas arguens: Quod si Christus (ut obloquuntur Marcionitæ) carne destitutus erat & exsanguis, cujusmodi Carnis, cujus corporis, qualis tandem sanguinis signa & IMAGINES PANEM ET POCULUM MINISTRAVIT. Dialog. 3. de Homine Christo.
